summary: Clarifies how implementations must handle unknown or unsupported flags in the Stateful PCE Request Parameters object of PCEP. RFC 8231 did not explain this, so the document sets updated rules.

eli5.summary: If a form has a checkbox you do not know about, this says what to do. Ignore it, or say no.

questions: how should pcep handle unknown srp flags
what are the stateful pce srp object rules
what is the pcep srp object
subtitle: Unassigned flags in the PCEP SRP object must be sent as zero and ignored when received.

tldr.problem: RFC 8231 gave the SRP object a 32-bit Flags field but did not say how to set unassigned flags when sending or how to handle unknown flags when receiving.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8786 updates RFC 8231 so that unassigned flags MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt, and an implementation that does not understand a flag MUST ignore it.
tldr.outcome: Old and new implementations can interoperate and future flags can be added safely. The RFC updates RFC 8231 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8786 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8231, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Gap in RFC 8231
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) carries messages between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE), or between PCEs. RFC 8231 adds extensions for stateful PCEs, including the Stateful PCE Request Parameters (SRP) object.

The SRP object has a Flags field of 32 bits, and RFC 8281 defines an IANA registry for tracking assigned flags. RFC 8231 did not say how to set unassigned flags in transmitted messages, nor how to process unassigned or unknown flags in received messages. It also gave no guidance to authors of future specifications on how new flags should interact with existing ones.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook gave the form a row of checkboxes but never said what to do with the ones nobody uses yet. This new rule fills that gap.

sections.title: The Updated Rules
sections.content:
Two pieces of RFC 8231 are replaced. First, in Section 7 the P and I flags of the PCEP objects MUST be set to 0 on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on receipt, since they relate only to path computation requests. Future specifications that define additional flags are expected to describe how the new flags interact with existing ones, especially when both are set.

Second, the SRP Flags text, which used to say "None defined yet", now reads: this document defines no flags; unassigned flags MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt; and implementations that do not understand a particular flag MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: Rule one: if a box has no meaning yet, leave it empty. Rule two: if you see a ticked box you do not know, pretend you did not see it.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content:
An implementation that follows RFC 8786 sets all unknown flag bits to zero, so it causes no problem for an older implementation even if that one inspects the bits. It also does not inspect unknown bits, so it is unaffected by how older implementations set them.

One risk remains. An RFC 8231 implementation might set an unassigned flag, while a current or future specification such as RFC 8281 or RFC 8741 gives that flag a meaning. The RFC says this cannot be fixed in old implementations. Since most implementations set unused flags to zero, the risk is small enough that there is no need to obsolete the Flags field.
sections.eli5: Most people already left unused boxes empty, so changing the rule rarely causes trouble. A few older programs might tick boxes by accident, but that is rare.

sections.title: Logging Unknown Flags
sections.content: An implementation that receives set SRP flags it does not recognize MAY log this. The RFC notes the log could help diagnose backward compatibility problems with future features that use those flags.
sections.eli5: If you meet a ticked box you do not know, you may write a note about it. The note can help someone work out later what went wrong.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
This document does not change the security considerations of RFC 8231. It says that defining expected behavior may improve network stability and so reduce the attack surface: ignoring unset bits makes it harder to attack implementations by randomly tweaking bits, and leaving undefined bits unset protects the network against new definitions of those bits.

For IANA, the reference for the "SRP Object Flag Field" subregistry of the PCEP Numbers registry was updated to list this document in addition to RFC 8281.
sections.eli5: When everyone follows the same rule, there are fewer surprises, so it is harder for a troublemaker to cause chaos by flipping random switches.
